# TADA at a glance {#tada}

**T**ransferable, **A**vailable, **D**ocumented, **A**nnotated. Four steps that
take analytical code from a working copy on one machine to an archived record
that another researcher can still run.

## Why another set of guidelines? {#tada-why}

There is no shortage of advice on writing good code, but very little of it deals
with the specific task of *archiving an analysis*.

The TADA authors identify three gaps in the existing resources:

1. They do not sufficiently address **how to archive analytical code**.
2. Few of them adhere to the **FAIR principles**.
3. Those that do, notably **FAIR4RS** (the FAIR principles for Research
   Software), are broad in scope and aimed at **software developers**, which may
   be part of why researchers have not widely adopted them.

Underlying all three is a distinction between *analytical code* and *software*.

**Software** is written to be general, modular and tested, and to work across
systems with many different compatible datasets. Designing for that kind of
reuse is genuinely complicated.

**Analytical code** is tailored to one dataset and one study. Its purpose is to
be a transparent, reproducible record of that analysis, not to become a tool for
other people.

Holding analytical code to software standards therefore sets an unrealistic
target, and researchers faced with an unrealistic target tend to give up on it entirely.
TADA instead sets a **minimum standard** that is achievable at any level of
coding experience while still delivering the transparency and computational
reproducibility that sharing is meant to provide.

## The scale of the problem {#tada-problem}

The numbers, all from the TADA paper's review of the literature, are
stark:

| What | Figure | Primary source |
|---|---|---|
| Journals in ecology & evolutionary biology with code-sharing policies | 15% in 2015, rising to **88% in 2024** | Mislan et al. 2016; Culina et al. 2020; Ivimey-Cook et al. 2025 |
| Articles in the field with open code | **5–35%**, depending on the study | various |
| Archived R files in Harvard Dataverse failing to run without error | **74%**, falling to 56% after automated cleaning | Trisovic et al. 2022 |
| Scripts in species distribution and abundance papers that did not run, or ran with errors | **93%** | Kellner et al. 2025 |
| Meta-analyses computationally reproducible given working data and code | between **27%** (every result matching exactly) and **73%** (half of results within 10%) | Kambouris et al. 2024 |

Journal policy has changed a great deal over the past decade; practice has been
much slower to follow. Even where code is present and does run, computational
reproducibility still cannot be assumed.

## The four principles {#tada-four}

Each has its own chapter. This is the one-paragraph version of each.

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[T]{.tada-letter} [Transferable](#transferable){.tada-word}
[Anyone can **open the file, view it and run it** without conversion or
alteration, on a different computer and a different operating system. Standard
file extensions, and no local file paths.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Available](#available){.tada-word}
[The code is **publicly archived** so that any external user has long-term
access to it, with a **globally unique persistent identifier** such as a DOI
that is cited in the manuscript.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[D]{.tada-letter} [Documented](#documented){.tada-word}
[**Accurate, detailed metadata**, typically a README, describing the code files
and their usage: environment, versions, licence, where the data are, and what
runs in what order.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Annotated](#annotated){.tada-word}
[**Comments inside the code**, or code embedded in RMarkdown or Quarto alongside
descriptive text, explaining what each chunk does, why it is needed and where
its output appears in the paper.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

## What TADA does not cover {#tada-scope}

The TADA paper is explicit that three things sit beyond its scope, while noting
that all three support reproducible analyses:

- **Dependency and environment managers** (`{renv}` in R, `{conda}` in Python),
  which help ensure the same computational environment is used each time, for
  example via a lockfile.
- **Containerisation** (Docker, Singularity), which packages a complete software
  environment of programs and libraries into an image so that the environment
  itself is reproducible between systems. This is the standard answer to the
  "works on my computer" problem.
- **Workflow managers** (Snakemake, Nextflow), which specify the sequence of
  scripts or computational steps in a pipeline and their dependencies, so that
  each step executes in a defined, reproducible order.

None of these is a requirement of TADA. All three are worth knowing about; see
[Further reading](#further-reading).

## How TADA maps onto FAIR {#tada-fair}

TADA was built with the FAIR and FAIR4RS principles in mind. Each letter maps
onto one or more of them, and in two cases deliberately goes further.

| FAIR principle | Definition | Covered by |
|---|---|---|
| **F**indable | Digital assets (metadata, data, code) can be easily found by both machines and humans | **Available**, through the provision of a unique identifier, and **Documented**, through the provision of rich metadata |
| **A**ccessible | Assets are retrievable via their identifier, with or without authorisation or authentication | **Available**, since the code is retrievable via that identifier |
| **I**nteroperable | Assets can interoperate with other assets, and are readable using standard documented formats | **Transferable**, *extended* to also mean runnable on different computers and operating systems |
| **R**eusable | Assets are described sufficiently to enable reuse and attribution, ideally via a licence | **Documented**, through a README and a licence, and **Annotated**, through commenting within the code itself |

::: {.tada-note}
All four rows are stated in the TADA paper, not inferred by the wiki. In the
paper's own words: Transferable "corresponds to the FAIR principle of
interoperability... and extends it"; Available "corresponds to the FAIR
principles of both Findable... and Accessible"; Documented "corresponds to...
the FAIR principle of Reusable... and Findable (the provision of rich
metadata)"; and Annotated, "similar to documentation, corresponds to the FAIR
principle of Reusable... but rather than describing the code 'externally',
provides clear commenting within each coding script." Documented and Annotated
therefore share the same FAIR principle (Reusable), distinguished only by
whether the description sits outside the code (a README) or inside it
(comments).
:::

**Transferable is broader than Interoperable.** Interoperability means anyone
can open and use your code. Transferability adds the requirement that it also
*runs* on someone else's machine and operating system, which is precisely where
hard-coded file paths cause problems.

**Annotated shares its FAIR principle with Documented, not with a principle of
its own.** Both map to Reusable, since both are ultimately about enabling
someone to understand and reuse the code; they differ in *where* that
description lives, externally in a README (Documented) or internally as
comments (Annotated). Annotated remains the letter most specific to research
code, in the sense that FAIR is largely concerned with machines finding and
parsing assets, whereas annotation is about a human being able to follow what
the analysis actually did — and it is the letter most often skipped.

::: {.tada-note}
On "reusable": the word is used in two different senses. In the FAIR sense it
means sharing code in a way that clearly specifies what can be done with it,
through a licence and a README. In the software-development sense it means
writing generalised, modular, tested code that runs across systems and datasets.
TADA targets the first. If you meet a guideline demanding the second, check
whether it was written for software.
:::

## Languages {#tada-languages}

TADA is tailored mainly to **R and Python**, because those are the open-source
languages most widely used in ecology and evolutionary biology. The basic
principles apply just as well to workflow languages such as Snakemake and
compiled languages such as C++ and, as the authors note, to disciplines other
than ecology and evolutionary biology.

Where a language does not save code in a standard file type, apply the
Transferable test: **can the resulting file be opened by a plain text editor?**
SPSS syntax `.sps` files, for instance, pass.
